questionText: Listen to a guided tour of a university campus given by a student ambassador.
audioScript:
Situation: A student ambassador leads a group of new undergraduates around the campus and points out key buildings and services.
Guide: Welcome, everyone, to Riverside University! I'm Priya, your campus ambassador today. We'll start at the main quadrangle behind me.
Student: Excuse me, where is the students' union building?
Guide: Good question. The students' union is the glass-fronted building to your left. It houses the café, a small supermarket, and the advice centre, open weekdays from nine until six.
Student: And where do first-year lectures usually take place?
Guide: Most first-year lectures are held in the Millbank Lecture Theatre, which is the red-brick building straight ahead. It seats three hundred students.
Student: Is there a place to print assignments nearby?
Guide: Yes, the print room is on the ground floor of the Learning Resource Centre, just past the library. Printing costs five pence per page for black and white.
Student: Great. What time does the sports centre close?
Guide: The sports centre stays open until ten on weekdays, and until eight at weekends. Remember to bring your student card to enter.
Student: Finally, where can we collect our student ID cards?
Guide: ID cards are issued at the registry, the white building next to the chapel. Bring your enrolment letter and a passport photo.

questionText: Listen to a librarian explaining the library services to a group of new students.
audioScript:
Situation: A university librarian addresses a group of new postgraduate students during a library orientation session.
Librarian: Welcome to the Hartwell Library. I'm Robert, your subject librarian for the sciences. Today I'll outline our key services.
Librarian: Our core collection spans four floors. The ground floor holds reference works that cannot be borrowed. The upper three floors hold the loanable collections.
Librarian: Undergraduates may borrow up to twelve books for two weeks. Postgraduates like yourselves may borrow up to twenty books for four weeks.
Student: Sorry, what happens if a book is overdue?
Librarian: Fines are fifty pence per day, capped at ten pounds per item. After two overdue notices, borrowing privileges are suspended.
Librarian: We also offer an inter-library loan service. Requests usually arrive within three working days and cost one pound each.
Librarian: For group study, you can book one of our six seminar rooms online. Each booking lasts up to two hours.
Librarian: Finally, our digital resources, including journal databases, are accessible off-campus using your university login. If you need help, drop in at the help desk on the ground floor between nine and five, Monday to Friday.

questionText: Listen to a museum guide giving a tour to a group of visitors.
audioScript:
Situation: A museum guide leads a group of visitors through the city museum and explains the exhibits and facilities.
Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside City Museum. I'm Margaret, your guide for today. We'll begin in the Egyptian gallery on this floor.
Visitor: Excuse me, how old is the oldest item here?
Guide: Great question. Our oldest exhibit is a clay tablet dating back three thousand years. It's displayed in the first case on your right.
Visitor: Are we allowed to take photographs?
Guide: You may take photos, but please do not use flash, as it can damage the fragile artefacts.
Visitor: Where can the children try the hands-on activities?
Guide: The interactive displays are on the second floor. They're very popular, especially the pottery-making station.
Visitor: How long will the guided tour take?
Guide: The tour lasts forty-five minutes, after which you're free to explore the rest of the museum at your own pace.
Visitor: Is there anything we can take away with us?
Guide: Yes, at the end of your visit you can collect a free souvenir guide from the front desk. It includes a map and highlights.
Visitor: We were told the museum has a free entry day. Which day is that?
Guide: Free entry is offered every Tuesday, from opening at ten until closing at six.
Visitor: One last question, where can we get some refreshments?
Guide: The museum café is on the ground floor, just next to the main entrance. It serves light lunches and hot drinks.
Visitor: And what time do you close on Sundays?
Guide: On Sundays we close at five in the afternoon, an hour earlier than weekdays.

questionText: Listen to a tour guide briefing visitors before a city walking tour begins.
audioScript:
Situation: A tour guide welcomes a group of visitors who have signed up for a guided walking tour of the city centre.
Guide: G'day, everyone! Welcome to City Steps Tours. My name is Lucy, and I'll be your guide for today. We'll be meeting right here, outside the central train station.
Visitor: Hi, how long will the walking tour take?
Guide: The tour runs for two hours, covering about three kilometres at a relaxed pace. We'll make several stops along the way.
Visitor: What's the first place we'll visit?
Guide: Our first stop is the old town hall, which was built in 1885. It's now used as a local history museum.
Visitor: Should we bring anything in particular?
Guide: Yes, please make sure you wear comfortable walking shoes and bring a water bottle, especially on hot days like today.
Visitor: How much does the tour cost per person?
Guide: The tour is fifteen dollars per person. Children under twelve can join for free with a paying adult.
Visitor: Where does the tour finish up?
Guide: We'll end the tour at the harbour, where there's a waterfront market. You can grab lunch or browse the stalls there.
Visitor: What time does the last tour of the day start?
Guide: The final tour departs at two in the afternoon. I'd recommend booking ahead, as it's quite popular.
Visitor: Is there a discount for groups?
Guide: Yes, groups of six or more receive a ten percent discount on the standard price.
Visitor: Great. And if it rains, do you still go ahead?
Guide: We do run in light rain, so bring an umbrella. If the weather is severe, we'll reschedule or offer a full refund.

questionText: Listen to an orientation coordinator briefing new students about orientation week activities.
audioScript:
Situation: An orientation coordinator addresses a group of new students to explain the schedule for the upcoming orientation week.
Coordinator: Welcome, everyone. I'm Sandra Williams, your orientation coordinator. Orientation week runs from Monday through Friday, with a packed schedule of activities designed to help you settle in.
Coordinator: On Monday, we'll start with campus tours departing from the main reception at ten. Each tour is led by a student ambassador.
Student: Where does the welcome ceremony take place?
Coordinator: The welcome ceremony is on Monday afternoon at two in the main auditorium. The vice-chancellor will give the opening address.
Student: I heard there's a society sign-up day. Do I need to do anything before that?
Coordinator: Yes. Before you attend the society sign-up day on Thursday, you must register online using your student portal account. This generates a barcode you'll need to scan at each stall.
Student: How many societies can I sign up for during orientation?
Coordinator: You can join up to three societies during orientation week. You're welcome to join more later in the term.
Student: Is there anything special for international students?
Coordinator: Absolutely. On Wednesday evening, we're hosting an international students' dinner in the dining hall. It's a great chance to meet people from different backgrounds.
Student: What about academic preparation? Is there a workshop?
Coordinator: Yes, the academic skills workshop is on Tuesday morning. You'll receive a study planner and timetable templates to help you organise your semester.
Student: What if I miss one of the registration sessions?
Coordinator: If you miss a session, please contact your faculty office directly. They'll help you arrange an alternative.
Student: And what happens on the last day?
Coordinator: Friday wraps up with a campus-wide treasure hunt followed by a barbecue on the lawn. It's always a highlight.

questionText: Listen to a hall warden presenting dormitory rules to new residents.
audioScript:
Situation: A hall warden addresses a group of new residents in a university dormitory to explain the rules and procedures.
Warden: Good evening, everyone. I'm Mr. Thompson, the warden of Elm Hall. I'd like to go over some essential house rules to make sure everyone has a safe and comfortable stay.
Warden: First, quiet hours run from ten o'clock in the evening until seven in the morning on weekdays. On weekends, quiet hours begin at midnight.
Student: Are we allowed to have guests stay overnight?
Warden: Yes, guests may stay overnight for a maximum of two nights per week. All guests must be signed in at the reception desk on arrival.
Student: Can we cook in our rooms?
Warden: I'm afraid not. Electrical cooking appliances such as kettles and hotplates are not permitted in student rooms due to fire safety. You're welcome to use the communal kitchen on each floor instead.
Student: How often do you have fire drills?
Warden: We conduct a fire drill once per term. When the alarm sounds at night, leave by the nearest exit and assemble at the car park at the rear of the building.
Student: What happens if I lose my room key?
Warden: If you lose your key, there's a twenty-pound replacement charge. Just visit reception during office hours.
Student: Who do we tell if something in our room is broken?
Warden: All maintenance issues should be reported to the maintenance team via the online portal. They aim to respond within forty-eight hours.
Student: Are there any rules about rubbish?
Warden: Yes, please use the recycling bins in the bin store next to the car park. General waste goes in the black bins and recyclables in the green bins.
Student: One more thing, is there a laundry room?
Warden: The laundry room is in the basement. Machines take a smart card which you top up online, not coins.

questionText: Listen to a campus security officer briefing new students on campus safety procedures.
audioScript:
Situation: A campus security officer speaks to a group of new students about safety services and emergency procedures on campus.
Officer: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Officer Davis from Campus Security. I'm here to walk you through our safety services and what to do in an emergency.
Officer: First and foremost, memorise our emergency number: five-five-five. Call it from any campus phone or mobile for any security concern.
Student: Where are the emergency call boxes located?
Officer: There are twenty-four call boxes placed along the main walkways and in all parking lots. They have a blue light on top so you can spot them easily at night.
Student: Is there a service for walking back to the dorm at night?
Officer: Yes, we offer a free campus escort service. A security staff member will walk with you from any campus building to your residence. The service runs from dusk until two in the morning.
Student: What should we do to keep our belongings safe?
Officer: Always lock your door, even if you're just stepping out briefly. Also, register your bicycle with us so we can identify it if it's recovered after being stolen.
Student: How will we know if there's a safety issue on campus?
Officer: We send campus safety alerts by email and text message as needed. Make sure your contact details are up to date in the student system.
Student: Where is the security office?
Officer: The security office is located next to the main parking structure, just behind the gym. We're open twenty-four hours a day.
Student: What about lockdown drills?
Officer: If a lockdown is announced, stay indoors, lock all doors, and await further instructions from security. Do not evacuate unless told to do so.
Student: Do you offer self-defence classes?
Officer: Yes, we run free self-defence workshops each semester. Sign up at the security office or through the campus portal.

questionText: Listen to a nurse explaining student health centre services to new students.
audioScript:
Situation: A senior nurse at the university health centre addresses new students to explain registration, appointments, and available medical services.
Nurse: Hello, everyone. I'm Dr. Patel, the senior physician here at the student health centre. I'll briefly explain how our services work so you know what to do when you need medical help.
Nurse: To register with us, you'll need to bring your student ID and a completed medical history form. You can pick up the form at reception or download it from the health centre website.
Student: Can we just walk in if we need to see a doctor?
Nurse: We have a walk-in clinic every weekday morning from nine until eleven. It's for minor ailments on a first-come, first-served basis.
Student: What about non-urgent appointments?
Nurse: For non-emergency appointments, please book online or by phone. This ensures you get a dedicated time slot with the right doctor.
Student: Is there a charge for seeing the doctor?
Nurse: Standard consultations are completely free for enrolled students. However, some specialist services carry a small fee.
Student: Are there any services that need a separate appointment?
Nurse: Yes, travel vaccinations require a separate appointment. Please book at least four weeks before you plan to travel, as some courses need multiple doses.
Student: What if I need to see a doctor urgently and the walk-in clinic is full?
Nurse: We reserve eight emergency appointments each day. These are only available if you call before ten in the morning.
Student: And what about urgent care after the health centre closes?
Nurse: For urgent care outside our hours, call the twenty-four-hour NHS helpline on one-one-one. They can advise you or direct you to the nearest service.
Student: How do prescriptions work?
Nurse: Once you order a prescription through our online system, it's valid for collection from the pharmacy for forty-eight hours. Just show your student ID when collecting.

questionText: Listen to a career advisor briefing students about an upcoming campus career fair.
audioScript:
Situation: A career advisor addresses a group of final-year students to explain the logistics and preparation for the upcoming campus career fair.
Advisor: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Ms. Chen from Career Services. I've organised this briefing to help you prepare for the career fair next week.
Advisor: We have fifty employers attending this year, ranging from tech companies to non-profits. The fair will be held in the Grand Hall of the conference centre, opening to students at ten in the morning.
Student: How should we prepare before the fair?
Advisor: First, bring several printed copies of your resume, at least ten. You should also research the employers you're most interested in beforehand.
Student: Is there a dress code?
Advisor: Yes, business attire is strongly recommended. First impressions matter, and recruiters do take note of how you present yourself.
Student: Are there any workshops before the fair?
Advisor: Yes, we're running a resume review session the day before the fair. Bring your current resume and a career advisor will give you one-on-one feedback.
Student: Can we do interviews at the fair?
Advisor: Some employers offer mini-interviews on the spot. Each slot is ten minutes long, and you can sign up at the employer's booth on the day.
Student: How can we find out which employers are coming in advance?
Advisor: You need to register on the career portal. Once registered, you'll have access to the full employer list and their profiles.
Student: What should we do after the fair?
Advisor: Follow up by sending a thank-you email to any recruiters you spoke with. You can also visit our career services drop-in desk for help with follow-up strategies and applications.
Student: Is the fair open to all students or just final-years?
Advisor: The fair is open to all year levels, but final-year students are especially encouraged to attend, as many employers are recruiting for graduate positions.

questionText: Listen to an advisor presenting information about studying abroad at a university info session.
audioScript:
Situation: A study abroad advisor gives an information session to second-year students considering a semester overseas.
Advisor: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Dr Helen Carter, the study abroad coordinator here at Westfield University. Today I'll walk you through the key steps for applying to study abroad in your third year.
Advisor: We currently partner with forty universities across eighteen countries. The most popular destinations are Canada, Australia, and Germany, but I'd encourage you to look beyond the obvious choices.
Advisor: Applications open on the first of October and close on the fifteenth of December. You'll need to submit a personal statement of five hundred words, two academic references, and your most recent transcript.
Student: Excuse me, is there a minimum grade requirement?
Advisor: Yes, you must hold at least a sixty per cent average in your current modules. Some partner universities ask for sixty-five, so check the specific requirements.
Advisor: There are two types of placement. The exchange programme means you pay no tuition fees to the host university, only your usual fees here. The study abroad programme means you pay tuition to the host institution directly.
Advisor: Funding is available through the Global Mobility Bursary, worth up to fifteen hundred pounds, awarded on a competitive basis. The deadline for bursary applications is the end of February.
Advisor: Finally, you must attend a pre-departure workshop in May, which covers visas, health insurance, and cultural adjustment. If you have questions afterwards, email me at the study abroad office.

Situation: A city transport officer briefs new university students on using public transport around the city.
Officer: Morning everyone. I'm Sandra, a transport officer with CityBus. I'm here to help you get around affordably as students. Let's cover the essentials.
Officer: The city has three main bus routes serving the university. The number seven runs every ten minutes and goes straight to the city centre. The number twelve runs every fifteen minutes and reaches the shopping district. The number twenty-three runs every twenty minutes and connects to the train station.
Student: How much does a single ticket cost?
Officer: A standard single is one pound eighty for adults, but with a student SmartCard it drops to one pound twenty.
Officer: I'd recommend the term pass. It costs ninety pounds and covers unlimited travel on all CityBus routes for thirteen weeks. Compared with pay-as-you-go, most students save about thirty pounds a term.
Officer: The SmartCard itself is free, but you need a passport photo and your student ID to register at the travel centre on Market Street. Registration takes about ten minutes.
Officer: Buses run from five in the morning until midnight, Monday to Saturday. On Sundays, services start at eight and finish at ten in the evening.
Officer: There's also a night bus, the N7, running every thirty minutes from midnight to four, mainly for safety. It follows the same route as the number seven but costs two pounds fifty regardless of your card.
Officer: Lost SmartCards can be replaced for a five-pound fee at the travel centre, and your remaining balance transfers automatically.

Situation: An academic integrity officer addresses a group of first-year postgraduate students to explain plagiarism, collusion, the penalties for academic misconduct, and how to avoid violations.
Officer: Good morning. I'm Professor Eleanor Bryant, the academic integrity officer at Kingsford University. This session is compulsory for all new postgraduate students, so please listen carefully.
Officer: Academic integrity means honesty and responsibility in all academic work. The three most common breaches are plagiarism, collusion, and contract cheating.
Student: Could you explain the difference between plagiarism and collusion?
Officer: Certainly. Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without proper acknowledgment. Collusion is when two or more students work together on an assignment that is meant to be completed individually.
Officer: Contract cheating is the most serious offence. This involves paying a third party, such as an essay mill, to produce work on your behalf. The minimum penalty for contract cheating is immediate expulsion from the university.
Student: What are the penalties for plagiarism?
Officer: Penalties depend on severity. For a first offence of minor plagiarism, the typical penalty is a mark of zero for the assignment and a mandatory training module. For repeat or serious offences, penalties can include failing the entire module or suspension.
Student: How can we avoid plagiarism?
Officer: Always cite your sources using the required referencing style. We use the Harvard system across most departments. Quotation marks must be used for direct quotes, and paraphrased ideas still require a citation.
Officer: All written submissions are checked through Turnitin, a similarity detection software. You will see a similarity score, but there is no fixed percentage that automatically triggers a penalty. Each case is reviewed individually by a panel.
Student: Can we work with classmates on homework?
Officer: Group discussion is encouraged, but unless your tutor explicitly permits collaborative submission, each student must write up their own answers independently. When in doubt, ask your tutor for clarification.

questionText: Listen to a campus security supervisor briefing staff on patrol procedures.
audioScript:
Situation: A campus security supervisor briefs a team of new patrol officers on procedures and protocols at the start of their shift.
Supervisor: Right, listen up. I'm Officer Daniels, your shift supervisor. This briefing covers our patrol procedures for the night shift, so pay close attention.
Supervisor: Our patrol route covers three zones. Zone A is the academic block, Zone B is the residential halls, and Zone C is the sports and recreation area. Each zone must be patrolled at least once every hour.
Officer: What should we do if we find a door that should be locked but isn't?
Supervisor: Good question. First, check whether anyone is inside. If the area is clear, secure the door and log the incident in the patrol report with the time and door number. If someone is inside, ask for their ID and verify they have authorisation.
Officer: And what's the protocol for dealing with suspicious individuals?
Supervisor: Approach calmly, identify yourself as campus security, and ask if they need assistance. If they refuse to cooperate or cannot give a reason for being on campus, call the control room immediately and do not attempt to detain them yourself.
Supervisor: For emergencies, use the code red over the radio. That triggers an immediate response from all nearby units. Code yellow means a non-urgent incident that still needs backup, like a reported theft.
Officer: What about medical emergencies?
Supervisor: For any medical situation, call an ambulance first, then radio code blue so the nearest first-aid-trained officer responds. Never move a seriously injured person unless they're in immediate danger.
Supervisor: Finally, all incidents must be written up in the logbook before the end of your shift. Reports submitted after seven in the morning are considered late and require a written explanation.

Situation: A university sustainability officer leads a group of students on a tour showcasing the campus's environmental initiatives and green infrastructure.
Officer: Hello, and welcome to the Green Campus Tour. I'm Dr. Eleanor Hayes, the sustainability officer here at Westwood University. Over the next hour, I'll show you how our campus is reducing its environmental footprint.
Officer: We'll begin at the solar panel array on the roof of the science block. Installed in 2021, these panels generate fifteen per cent of the university's electricity, saving approximately two hundred tonnes of carbon emissions annually.
Student: That's impressive. Is there more renewable infrastructure?
Officer: Indeed. Next, we have the rainwater harvesting system beneath the engineering building. It collects runoff from rooftops and irrigates the campus lawns and gardens. In a typical year, the system saves around one million litres of mains water.

Officer: Yes, our new student centre, opened last spring, is a showcase. It's constructed almost entirely from locally sourced, recycled materials, including reclaimed timber and recycled steel. The design prioritises natural light and ventilation.
Officer: Over to your right, you'll notice the biodiversity garden. Its main purpose is to attract and protect native pollinators, such as bees and butterflies, by providing the right wildflowers and habitats. Student volunteers help maintain it.
Student: Is there a way to get around campus without a car?
Officer: Absolutely. We run a bicycle hire scheme. Students can register online for a free annual membership, which allows unlimited borrowing from bike stations across campus. It's proven very popular.
Officer: Our environmental policy, approved by the university senate, pledges to reduce waste sent to landfill by fifty per cent within five years. We're currently in year three and on track to meet that target.
Officer: Finally, all of this is documented in our campus sustainability report, which is published annually and available on the university website. It tracks our progress against every target I've mentioned today.

questionText: Listen to a mentorship programme coordinator introducing the student mentorship scheme to first-year students.

Situation: A mentorship programme coordinator introduces the university's student mentorship scheme to an audience of first-year students at an induction event.
Coordinator: Good morning, everyone. I'm Professor James Aldridge, and I coordinate the Bridges Mentorship Programme here at Thornfield University. Let me explain how it works.
Coordinator: The programme pairs each first-year student with a trained mentor from the third or fourth year. Mentors provide academic guidance, social support, and help you navigate university life during your first two semesters.
Student: How do we get matched with a mentor?
Coordinator: Great question. You'll complete an online questionnaire that asks about your course, interests, and any preferences, such as same-gender matching. Our algorithm then pairs you within forty-eight hours, and you'll receive your mentor's contact details by email.
Student: How often are we supposed to meet?
Coordinator: We ask mentors and mentees to meet face-to-face at least twice a month, for about an hour each time. You can also contact your mentor by email or message between meetings, but mentors aren't expected to reply outside working hours.
Coordinator: Mentors receive training in active listening, safeguarding, and signposting to university services. They are not counsellors, so if you're dealing with a serious issue, they'll refer you to the appropriate professional service.
Student: What if we don't get along with our mentor?
Coordinator: That does happen occasionally. You can request a reassignment through the programme portal within the first six weeks, no questions asked. After six weeks, requests are reviewed case by case.
Coordinator: At the end of the year, both mentors and mentees submit a short reflection report. Mentees who complete the programme receive a certificate that can be added to your higher education achievement report, which is useful for job applications.
Coordinator: Registration opens today and closes on the twentieth of September. There's no cost, but places are limited to three hundred mentees, so I encourage you to sign up promptly.
